claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially exists as a high-temperature, single-phase BCC alloy.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the temperature-dependent Gibbs free-energy difference between BCC and FCC.
The Gibbs free-energy difference between BCC and FCC can be a critical parameter for phase transformation.
CALPHAD predicts a critical temperature-dependent change in ΔG_bcc-fcc for Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Cooling causes the calculated ΔG_bcc-fcc to decrease.
A sufficiently negative ΔG_bcc-fcc makes FCC thermodynamically favored over BCC.
Below a critical temperature, the thermodynamic driving force causes a BCC-to-FCC transformation in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
BCC and FCC phase fractions evolve in correspondence with thermodynamic phase stability as composition and temperature vary.
Crossing the predicted thermodynamic threshold will reduce the BCC fraction and increase the FCC fraction.
Rapid cooling retains the high-temperature BCC phase by kinetically suppressing transformation.
Samples treated where ΔG_bcc-fcc is sufficiently negative will have more FCC and less BCC than rapidly cooled samples.
The thermodynamic database used for the CALPHAD calculations is not accurate below 0 °C.
At very low temperatures or under nonequilibrium conditions, kinetic barriers may delay or alter the predicted transformation.
The exact transformation temperature and ΔG threshold are uncertain because of kinetic hindrance and discrepancies between CALPHAD predictions and actual kinetics.
Controlled thermal treatments should systematically traverse the predicted transformation range and be compared with rapidly cooled samples.
XRD and electron microscopy can be used to quantify or verify the BCC and FCC phase fractions after treatment.
DSC can detect latent heat associated with the proposed phase transformation.
Failure to observe increased FCC at the CALPHAD-predicted threshold would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule treats failure to transform at the predicted temperature as falsifying, whereas the boundary and uncertainty fields allow the same failure or displacement to result from kinetic barriers or CALPHAD–kinetics discrepancies. No criterion distinguishes a true thermodynamic falsification from an allowed kinetic delay.
